  /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/mm/mm.c

Use 'git diff' in /workspace to see exactly what was added (the rest of the tree is pre-existing scaffolding).
Read supporting headers (include/os/*.h, arch/riscv/include/pgtable.h, drivers/net.h, kernel/syscall/syscall.c, init/main.c, test/*.c) to understand the intended contracts.
Both projects already COMPILE cleanly, so do not report compile errors unless you are certain.
Report only real correctness defects that would cause wrong behavior at runtime. Be concrete and cite file:line.
Focus dimension: Demand paging and swapping in P4 mm.c — selete_page (NRU victim selection using the A/D accessed/dirty bits, must skip pinned pages, must clear A bits periodically, must not select a page belonging to the page-table structure itself), write_to_sd (choosing a free swap sector, sbi_sd_write of the 4KB page = 8 sectors, recording the swap location in the now-invalid PTE, invalidating the PTE and flushing TLB via sfence), and handle_page_fault (distinguishing load/store/instruction page faults from the scause cause code, swap-in from disk, correctly restoring PTE flags, handling COW/shared memory, killing the process on a genuinely invalid address).

id: "p4_virtual_memory"
title: "Project 4 — Virtual Memory Management"
category: os
requirement: |-
  ## Context
  This is a operating-systems course lab (Projects 1–6) that implements a RISC-V bare-metal operating system. The repo spans six incremental projects: a bootloader, a simple cooperative kernel, a preemptive kernel with SMP, an interactive OS with process management and IPC, a virtual-memory-enabled kernel with demand paging, a device-driver layer with network support, and a file system. Entire subsystems have been removed and must be re-implemented.

  Your working directory is `/workspace`. The project code is already present in seven subdirectories: `Project1-Bootloader`, `Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1`, `Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part2`, `Project3-Interactive_OS_and_Process_Management`, `Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management`, `Project5-Device_Driver`, and `Project6-File_System`.

  ## Module: Project 4 — Virtual Memory Management
  Adds SV39 three-level page table management (init_page_table, free_process_user_page), NRU page replacement (selete_page), swap-to-disk eviction (write_to_sd), demand-paging page fault handler (handle_page_fault), user page allocation (alloc_user_page), shared memory mapping (shm_page_get, shm_page_dt), and ELF binary loading (do_exec). The sched.c evolves P3's process management with virtual address space integration.

  ## Files to modify
  Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/

SHELL := /bin/bash
HOST_CC = gcc
CROSS_PREFIX = riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu-
CC = ${CROSS_PREFIX}gcc
AR = ${CROSS_PREFIX}ar
OBJDUMP = ${CROSS_PREFIX}objdump
CFLAGS = -O0 -nostdlib -T riscv.lds -Wall -mcmodel=medany -Iinclude -Idrivers -nostdinc -g -fvar-tracking -ffreestanding
USER_CFLAGS = -O0 -nostdlib -T user_riscv.lds -Wall -mcmodel=medany -Itest -Itiny_libc/include -Iinclude -nostdinc -g -fvar-tracking
USER_LDFLAGS = -L./ -ltiny_libc
DISK = /dev/sdb

BOOTLOADER_ENTRYPOINT = 0x50200000
START_ENTRYPOINT = 0x50201000
KERNEL_ENTRYPOINT = 0xffffffc050400000

ARCH = riscv
ARCH_DIR = ./arch/$(ARCH)
CFLAGS += -Iarch/$(ARCH)/include
USER_CFLAGS += -Iarch/$(ARCH)/include
USER_LDFLAGS += $(ARCH_DIR)/crt0.o

SRC_BOOT 	= $(ARCH_DIR)/boot/bootblock.S
SRC_HEAD    = $(ARCH_DIR)/kernel/head.S $(ARCH_DIR)/kernel/boot.c payload.c ./libs/string.c
SRC_ARCH	= $(ARCH_DIR)/kernel/trap.S $(ARCH_DIR)/kernel/entry.S $(ARCH_DIR)/kernel/start.S $(ARCH_DIR)/sbi/common.c $(ARCH_DIR)/kernel/smp.S
SRC_DRIVER	= ./drivers/screen.c
SRC_INIT 	= ./init/main.c
SRC_INT		= ./kernel/irq/irq.c
SRC_LOCK	= ./kernel/locking/lock.c ./kernel/locking/futex.c ./kernel/locking/binsem.c
SRC_SCHED	= ./kernel/sched/sched.c ./kernel/sched/time.c ./kernel/sched/smp.c
SRC_MM	    = ./kernel/mm/mm.c
SRC_SYSCALL	= ./kernel/syscall/syscall.c ./kernel/syscall/mailbox.c
SRC_LIBS	= ./libs/string.c ./libs/printk.c

SRC_LIBC	= ./tiny_libc/printf.c ./tiny_libc/string.c ./tiny_libc/mthread.c ./tiny_libc/syscall.c ./tiny_libc/invoke_syscall.S \
				./tiny_libc/time.c ./tiny_libc/mailbox.c ./tiny_libc/rand.c ./tiny_libc/atol.c
SRC_LIBC_ASM	= $(filter %.S %.s,$(SRC_LIBC))
SRC_LIBC_C	= $(filter %.c,$(SRC_LIBC))

SRC_USER	= ./test/test_shell.elf ./test/rw.elf ./test/fly.elf ./test/consensus.elf ./test/swap.elf

SRC_MAIN	= ${SRC_ARCH} ${SRC_INIT} ${SRC_INT} ${SRC_DRIVER} ${SRC_LOCK} ${SRC_SCHED} ${SRC_MM} ${SRC_SYSCALL} ${SRC_LIBS}

SRC_IMAGE	= ./tools/createimage.c
SRC_ELF2CHAR	= ./tools/elf2char.c
SRC_GENMAP	= ./tools/generateMapping.c

.PHONY:all main bootblock clean

all: elf2char createimage image asm

bootblock: $(SRC_BOOT) riscv.lds
	${CC} ${CFLAGS} -o bootblock $(SRC_BOOT) -e main -Ttext=${BOOTLOADER_ENTRYPOINT}

kernelimage: $(SRC_HEAD) riscv.lds
	${CC} ${CFLAGS} -o kernelimage $(SRC_HEAD) -Ttext=${START_ENTRYPOINT}

payload.c: elf2char main
	./elf2char main > payload.c

user: $(SRC_USER) elf2char generateMapping
	echo "" > user_programs.c
	echo "" > user_programs.h
	for prog in $(SRC_USER); do ./elf2char --header-only $$prog >> user_programs.h; done
	for prog in $(SRC_USER); do ./elf2char $$prog >> user_programs.c; done
	./generateMapping user_programs
	mv user_programs.h include/

#include <sbi.h>
#include <atomic.h>
#include <os/sched.h>
#include <os/smp.h>
#include <os/lock.h>
#include <os/irq.h>

struct spin_lock kernel_lock;
int smp_init_flag = 0;

void smp_init()
{
    PTE *pgdir = (PTE*)PGDIR_PA;
    *(pgdir + 0x001) = 0;
    smp_init_flag = 1;

    enable_interrupt();
    setup_exception();
    sbi_set_timer(get_ticks() + timer_interval);
    while (1){
        __asm__ __volatile__("wfi\n\r":::);
    }
}

void wakeup_other_hart()
{
    sbi_send_ipi(NULL);
}

void lock_kernel()
{
    spin_lock_acquire(&kernel_lock);
}

void unlock_kernel()
{
    spin_lock_release(&kernel_lock);
}=== entry.S ===

content.text: I've reviewed the demand-paging/swapping paths in P4 `mm.c` (plus the P5 twin) against the headers, trap dispatch, boot page tables, and the test programs. Here are the defects I can substantiate.

findings.title: A user-mode fault on a kernel address hangs the entire OS instead of killing the process
findings.detail: handle_page_fault() routes every fault whose stval is outside the Sv39 user half to handle_other() (mm.c:399-401). handle_other() (kernel/irq/irq.c:63-105) dumps registers, walks the user frame pointer chain, and finishes with assert(0), which expands to _panic() -> `for(;;);` (include/assert.h:8). Because the trap entry took the big kernel lock (arch/riscv/kernel/entry.S:199) and never reaches the `call unlock_kernel` at entry.S:157, the spinning hart also keeps the lock, so the second hart wedges on its next trap. A wild user pointer, a non-sign-extended address, or an explicit access to a kernel VA therefore takes the whole machine down.
findings.why_wrong: A page fault taken in U-mode at an address the process may not touch is a user error, not a kernel error; the contract for this lab is to terminate the offending process (do_exit/do_kill) and keep the system running. Nothing in handle_page_fault inspects the privilege the fault was taken from (regs->sstatus SPP) before deciding to panic. This is directly reachable from the shipped `rw` test: test/rw.c:16-19 does `*(long*)atol(argv[i]) = ...` on a shell-supplied address, so `exec rw 274877906944` (2^38) or any larger value freezes the OS instead of reporting a fault.
findings.suggested_fix: Split the decision on the fault's privilege level: if `(regs->sstatus & SR_SPP) == 0` (U-mode) and the address is not a legal user address, print a diagnostic and terminate the current process (e.g. `do_exit()` / mark it for destruction and call scheduler()) rather than calling handle_other(). Reserve handle_other()/panic for S-mode faults.

findings.title: handle_page_fault never rejects an invalid address: any user VA below 2^38 is silently backed by a fresh zero page
findings.detail: After the >= 2^38 check, the handler unconditionally calls alloc_page_helper(stval, current_running[cpu_id]->pgdir) (mm.c:406). There is no test against the process's legal regions (code 0xf000-0x14000, the shm window 0x1000-0xf000, the stack below USER_STACK_ADDR), and no notion of an unmapped hole. A NULL dereference at VA 0 is turned into a readable/writable/executable user page (flags set at mm.c:233-234) and the faulting instruction simply succeeds.
findings.why_wrong: Demand paging is supposed to distinguish "valid but not resident" from "never mapped". Here every one of the 2^38 user addresses is treated as valid-but-not-resident, so (a) genuine program bugs are masked instead of killing the process, and (b) a runaway process can consume all 53248 user frames and then all 256 swap slots, at which point `assert(i != DISK_PAGE_NUM)` in write_to_sd (mm.c:131) or `assert(0)` in selete_page (mm.c:119) panics the kernel — an unprivileged process can hang the machine. It also affects kernel threads: kernel_pcb[*].pgdir == PGDIR_PA (init/main.c:77,92), so a low-address dereference by a kernel task makes walk_pgdir install user-accessible RWX mappings into the global kernel page table at PGDIR_PA instead of reporting the bug.
findings.suggested_fix: Track each process's valid VA ranges (code/data extent recorded by load_elf, the shm window, and a stack region bounded by a max stack size) and only call alloc_page_helper for addresses inside them; otherwise kill the process. At minimum reject VA 0 / the first page, reject addresses between the top of the loaded image and the stack guard, and never demand-map into pgdir == PGDIR_PA.

findings.title: Page-fault handler makes no forward progress when the leaf PTE is already present, producing an infinite trap loop
findings.detail: alloc_page_helper's entire body is guarded by `if(!get_attribute(*pte, _PAGE_PRESENT))` (mm.c:218-236). When the fault was raised on a PTE that is already valid — a permission or A/D-bit fault rather than a "not present" fault — the function does nothing and returns the existing kva. handle_page_fault (mm.c:406) discards that return value and returns without touching regs->sepc, so ret_from_exception re-executes the same instruction, which faults identically. The hart then spins in the trap handler forever, re-acquiring and releasing the kernel lock on every iteration. The `cause` argument is never examined, so EXCC_INST_PAGE_FAULT (12), EXCC_LOAD_PAGE_FAULT (13) and EXCC_STORE_PAGE_FAULT (15) — all wired to this handler in kernel/irq/irq.c:37-39 — are indistinguishable.
findings.why_wrong: Two reachable triggers exist. (1) shm_page_get maps shared pages with `_PAGE_PRESENT|_PAGE_READ|_PAGE_WRITE|_PAGE_USER|_PAGE_ACCESSED|_PAGE_DIRTY` and deliberately no `_PAGE_EXEC` (mm.c:353-354); an instruction fetch from a shared page raises an instruction page fault on a present PTE and hangs the process. (2) selete_page clears `_PAGE_ACCESSED` on live PTEs (mm.c:112); on any RISC-V implementation that does not do hardware A/D updating (the privileged spec explicitly permits raising a page fault instead, and Svadu is an optional extension), the very next access to that page traps on a present PTE and the process wedges. In both cases the handler cannot even report the error because it never inspects `cause`.
findings.suggested_fix: Decode `cause` in handle_page_fault. For a fault on a PTE that is already `_PAGE_PRESENT`, set `_PAGE_ACCESSED` (and `_PAGE_DIRTY` for EXCC_STORE_PAGE_FAULT), sfence, and return; if the required permission bit (R for load, W for store, X for instruction) is genuinely absent, kill the process instead of returning to the same instruction. Have alloc_page_helper report whether it changed anything so the caller can detect the no-progress case.

findings.title: Swap-out and unmap only flush the local TLB on a 2-hart SMP kernel, leaving stale writable translations on the other hart
findings.detail: P5's write_to_sd invalidates the victim's PTE and then calls only `local_flush_tlb_all()` (mm.c:161), and the same local-only flush is used after tearing down an address space (mm.c:269), after installing a new mapping (mm.c:346) and after detaching a shared page (mm.c:400). include/os/smp.h:4 sets NR_CPUS 2 and init/main.c:234 starts the second hart, and `sbi_remote_sfence_vma()` is available at arch/riscv/include/sbi.h:104 but is never used. P4 gets this right — its pgtable.h provides `flush_tlb_all()` (local sfence + `sbi_remote_sfence_vma`) and P4's mm.c uses it at lines 147, 235, 332, 356, 383 — so the P5 copy of the same code silently dropped the remote shootdown.
findings.why_wrong: The big kernel lock is only held while a hart is inside the kernel (entry.S acquires it on trap entry and releases it before sret), so hart 1 can be executing user code of process X while hart 0 is inside alloc_user_page -> selete_page -> write_to_sd evicting one of X's pages. After the local-only sfence, hart 1's TLB still holds the old valid, writable translation. write_to_sd then calls free_user_page (mm.c:162), the frame is immediately handed to another process by alloc_user_page, memset to zero and filled with that process's data — while hart 1 keeps reading and writing the same physical frame through its stale TLB entry. The result is silent cross-process memory corruption; the same hazard applies to free_process_user_page and shm_page_dt, where the frame is likewise recycled right after a local-only flush.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the `local_flush_tlb_all()` calls at Project5-Device_Driver/kernel/mm/mm.c:161, 269, 346 and 400 with a helper that also broadcasts the shootdown, e.g. add `static inline void flush_tlb_all(void){ local_flush_tlb_all(); sbi_remote_sfence_vma(NULL, 0, -1); }` to Project5-Device_Driver/arch/riscv/include/pgtable.h (mirroring the P4 version) and call it. The `local_flush_tlb_all()` after set_satp in kernel/sched/sched.c:96 is fine and can stay local.

findings.title: selete_page clears _PAGE_ACCESSED without invalidating the TLB, so the reference bit is never re-set and NRU degenerates
findings.detail: The clock sweep clears `_PAGE_ACCESSED` in the leaf PTE (mm.c:112) and moves on. No `local_flush_tlb_page`/`flush_tlb_all` is issued for that VA, and write_to_sd's flush at mm.c:147 only happens for the page that is finally evicted, not for the pages that were given a second chance.
findings.why_wrong: The hardware only writes the A bit back to memory when it performs a page-table walk. As long as the translation stays cached in the TLB the MMU never re-walks, so the A bit that was just cleared in memory stays 0 no matter how hot the page is. Consequently, on the second sweep of the `2 * USER_PAGE_NUM` loop every page the first sweep cleared appears unreferenced and the very first candidate is evicted. The intended NRU/second-chance policy collapses into "evict whatever the clock hand points at", which is what the requirement for A-bit-based victim selection is meant to avoid, and it causes needless eviction of the actively-used working set.
findings.suggested_fix: Issue a shootdown for the page whose A bit was just cleared before continuing the sweep — either `flush_tlb_page_all(va)` (the VA can be reconstructed if you also store it in user_page_t) or a single `flush_tlb_all()` at the end of each sweep pass, so the next access re-walks and re-sets the A bit.

findings.title: The dirty bit is never consulted: every eviction performs a full 8-sector write even for clean pages
findings.detail: selete_page classifies victims using only `_PAGE_ACCESSED` (mm.c:111) and write_to_sd unconditionally issues `sbi_sd_write(pa, 8, SWAP_BEGIN + i*8)` (mm.c:134). `_PAGE_DIRTY` is set eagerly on every mapping at mm.c:233-234 and on every shared mapping at mm.c:353-354, and is never cleared anywhere, so it carries no information at all.
findings.why_wrong: The requirement is NRU over the (A, D) pair, which both ranks victims by the four A/D classes and lets a clean page be dropped without an SD write (read-only text pages in particular can be re-faulted from the ELF image or from their existing swap slot). As implemented, a clean page costs a 4 KB synchronous SD write on every eviction, and a page that is repeatedly swapped in and out is rewritten each time even though its contents never changed. It also means a page swapped in at mm.c:223 and never written is given a brand-new slot on its next eviction instead of reusing the identical on-disk copy.
findings.suggested_fix: Clear `_PAGE_DIRTY` (with a TLB shootdown) when a page is mapped or swapped in, rank victims by the (A, D) class as NRU prescribes, and in write_to_sd skip the sbi_sd_write when D is clear and a valid swap slot for that PTE already exists.

findings.title: The kernel holds a direct-map pointer into an unpinned frame across operations that can evict it
findings.detail: init_user_stack obtains `top_kva` for the child's stack frame at sched.c:160-161 via alloc_page_helper, which allocates with `alloc_user_page(0, pte)` — pin = 0 (mm.c:222/229). It then reads the parent's user memory through `strlen(argv[i])` at sched.c:178 and `memcpy(..., argv[i], ...)` at sched.c:189, with SUM enabled by do_exec, while continuing to write into the child's frame through `STACK_KVA(...)`.
findings.why_wrong: Those reads of `argv[i]` are ordinary user-space accesses and can take a page fault, which re-enters handle_page_fault -> alloc_page_helper -> alloc_user_page -> selete_page/write_to_sd. Under memory pressure selete_page is free to pick the child's stack frame: it is valid, pin == 0 and reachable through a PTE (mm.c:122), so nothing protects it. write_to_sd then flushes it to disk and calls free_user_page, and the frame is handed to another process. init_user_stack keeps writing the argv strings and pointer array through the now-stale `top_kva`, corrupting the new owner's page, while the child's stack page is restored from swap holding the zeros it had before the copy — so the child receives a garbage argv. The same exposure applies to any kva returned by alloc_page_helper that is kept live across another allocation.
findings.suggested_fix: Pin frames while the kernel holds a direct-map pointer into them: give alloc_page_helper a pin flag (or set user_page[pa2num(pa)].pin = 1 around the critical region and clear it afterwards) for the child's stack page in init_user_stack, and copy the argv strings into a kernel-local buffer before any user access that can fault.
